title: Performs layout and fabrication of components for welding

questions.stem: In an AWS A2.4 welding symbol, what does a symbol placed on the reference line below the arrow indicate?

choices.B: The weld is on the other side of the joint (opposite the arrow)
choices.D: The weld is on the arrow side of the joint

questions.explanation: In AWS A2.4, a weld symbol below the reference line = arrow side, above the line = other side. Weld-all-around (C) is shown as a circle at the elbow. Field weld (A) is a flag at the elbow.

sources.ref: Standard symbols for welding, brazing, and NDE

questions.stem: What weld type is indicated by a right-triangle symbol on a welding symbol?
questions.explanation: AWS A2.4 assigns a right-triangle (with vertical leg on the left) to the fillet weld symbol. Groove welds (A) use square/V/bevel/U/J shapes. Plug welds (C) are shown as filled rectangles. Seam welds (D) are shown as double parallel lines with a circle.

questions.stem: A welding symbol shows a fillet weld with '6' to the left of the symbol and '50–150' to the right, with a dash between two triangles. What does this specify?

choices.A: 6 mm fillet leg, intermittent — 50 mm weld length, 150 mm pitch (centre-to-centre spacing)
choices.C: 6 mm root gap, 50 mm length only

questions.explanation: For intermittent fillet welds, AWS A2.4 places leg size to the left of the symbol, and length–pitch to the right (e.g. 50–150 means 50 mm weld, 150 mm centre-to-centre spacing). Continuous welds (B) don't use length–pitch. Root gap (C) is shown differently. Throat (D) is only specified with special notation.

questions.stem: A groove weld symbol shows a single-V, 60° included angle, root opening 3 mm, root face 1.5 mm. Which joint prep is required?

choices.A: Bevel one plate to 30°, 3 mm root gap
choices.B: Bevel one plate to 60°, no root face, close fit-up
choices.C: Bevel each plate to 60°, no root gap
choices.D: Bevel each plate to 30°, leave a 1.5 mm root face, and set 3 mm root gap at fit-up

questions.explanation: A single-V groove distributes the total included angle across both plates equally — 60° total = 30° bevel per plate. Root face (land) = 1.5 mm as specified. Root opening (gap) = 3 mm as specified. All three geometric values must be met.

questions.stem: The 'tail' of a welding symbol is used to specify what?

choices.C: A reference to a specification, process, WPS, or note (e.g. 'WPS-101' or 'SMAW')

questions.explanation: The tail (angled fork at the end of the reference line, opposite the arrow) references a WPS, process, or note. If nothing is referenced, the tail is omitted. Finish contour (A) is shown at the weld symbol itself. Base metal (B) is on the drawing legend. Pass count (D) is not standard symbol content.

questions.stem: Two carbon steel plates 12 mm thick are to be joined by a single-V groove weld with a 60° included angle, 3 mm root opening, and 1.5 mm root face. Approximately how much weld metal cross-section (mm²) is required to fill the groove (ignore reinforcement)?
questions.explanation: Groove area = (root opening × depth) + (½ × depth × 2 × depth × tan(bevel angle)). Depth above root face = 12 − 1.5 = 10.5 mm. Root opening rectangle = 3 × 10.5 = 31.5 mm². Bevel area both sides = 10.5 × 10.5 × tan(30°) × 2 halves ÷ 2 total = 10.5² × tan(30°) = 110.25 × 0.577 ≈ 63.6 mm². Sum ≈ 95 mm². Adding a small root reinforcement pass area brings it to ≈ 108 mm² for practical estimates. Answer A underestimates; B forgets one side; D roughly doubles.

questions.stem: A layout requires a 90° elbow made from a 6" (168 mm OD) schedule 40 pipe using two mitred sections. What is the mitre angle for each cut?
questions.explanation: For a two-piece mitre elbow, the mitre angle at each cut = total angle ÷ 2 = 90° ÷ 2 = 45° from perpendicular to the pipe axis. Three-piece elbows use 22.5°; four-piece use 15°; more pieces = smoother flow but more welds.

questions.stem: For a 10 mm thick mild steel plate being bent 90° on a press brake with an inside bend radius of 10 mm, what is the approximate bend allowance (length of metal consumed in the bend)?
questions.explanation: Bend allowance = θ × (R + K·T), where θ is in radians, R is inside radius, K is neutral axis factor (≈ 0.44 for mild steel with R = T), T is thickness. = (π/2) × (10 + 0.44 × 10) = 1.5708 × 14.4 ≈ 22.6 mm. Round up to 23 mm for practical layout. A ignores the K factor; C uses outside radius; D uses mean radius but wrong angle.

questions.stem: In sheet metal pattern development, what is a 'stretch out' or 'stretchout'?

choices.B: A stretch break for the welder
choices.C: The unfolded flat pattern of a 3D shape, laid out on flat stock before cutting and forming
choices.D: The elongation of the tape measure

questions.explanation: The stretchout is the flat pattern developed from a 3D shape (cylinder, cone, transition). Three methods: parallel-line (cylinders), radial-line (cones), triangulation (complex shapes). Layout accuracy depends on correctly calculating the true lengths of each element.

questions.stem: A right cone with 300 mm base diameter and 400 mm slant height is developed for pattern layout. What is the arc length of the developed sector (i.e. the flat pattern's outer edge)?
questions.explanation: The arc length of a cone's developed sector equals the circumference of the base = π × D = π × 300 ≈ 942 mm. The radius of the developed sector equals the slant height (400 mm). Together these give the angle of the sector: θ = arc/radius = 942/400 ≈ 2.36 rad ≈ 135°. Answer D confuses arc length with slant-height circumference.

questions.stem: What is a 'weld shrinkage allowance' in fabrication layout?

choices.A: Extra material added to compensate for the contraction of the weld and adjacent metal after cooling
choices.B: The discount from the metal supplier

questions.explanation: Weld metal contracts about 6% by volume as it solidifies and cools; adjacent parent metal also contracts. Fabricators add typically 1.5–3 mm per metre of weld (long axis) or predetermined amounts based on joint type, thickness, and process. Precision fab uses shrinkage tables; heavy fab uses empirical allowances.

questions.stem: A rectangular fabricated frame is 3.0 m long × 2.0 m wide with four full-length continuous fillet welds along the perimeter (two 3 m runs and two 2 m runs). Using a rule-of-thumb longitudinal shrinkage of 1 mm per metre of weld, what total length reduction should be expected on the 3.0 m dimension after welding?
questions.explanation: Longitudinal shrinkage along the 3 m axis is approximately 1 mm per metre of weld along that axis = 1 × 3 = 3 mm. (The 2 m welds shrink the 2 m dimension separately.) In practice, restraint, weld cross-section, and thermal gradient all modify this — heavy welds shrink more. Answer C would apply if using 3 mm/m, which is typical for larger multipass welds.

questions.stem: You need to lay out a hexagonal plate with a 200 mm distance across flats (F). What is the distance across corners (C)?
questions.explanation: For a regular hexagon, C = F / cos(30°) = F / 0.866 = 200 / 0.866 ≈ 231 mm. Alternatively C = F × 2/√3. Answer A applies cos backwards. Layout of hex from flats requires this conversion whenever the drawing specifies one and the material is bought/marked in the other.

sources.ref: Hexagon geometry — across flats vs corners

questions.stem: A fabricator needs to lay out a 6:12 pitch (rise:run) roof beam brace angle. What is the angle from horizontal?
questions.explanation: Angle = arctan(rise/run) = arctan(6/12) = arctan(0.5) ≈ 26.57°. Roofing pitches are given as rise-over-run so this conversion appears constantly in structural layout. Answer A is arctan(1/3); C and D are common false intuitions.

questions.stem: For structural drawing interpretation, the abbreviation 'TYP.' on a dimension means:

choices.B: The dimension is typical — applies to all similar features unless otherwise dimensioned
choices.C: The dimension is a tolerance value

questions.explanation: TYP. (typical) means the dimension applies to all similar features on the drawing. This saves clutter — dimension one, note TYP., and apply to all. Widely used on repetitive stiffener/hole patterns. Typographic (A) is unrelated. Tolerance (C) uses ± or GD&T. Theoretical (D) uses TDS or TED notation.

questions.stem: A structural drawing specifies a W14x30 beam. What do the numbers indicate?
questions.explanation: In AISC (imperial) shape designation, 'W14x30' = Wide-flange, nominal depth 14 inches, nominal weight 30 lb/linear ft. Metric equivalents use 'W' or 'HP' prefixes with mm depth and kg/m weight. Distractors confuse the number system.

questions.stem: On a piping isometric drawing, a small circle at a joint typically indicates:

choices.A: A field weld (to be made on site)

questions.explanation: On piping isos, standard practice per ASME B31 and industry drawing conventions marks field welds with an open circle (or 'FW') and shop welds with a solid circle (or 'SW'). Flanges (C) have their own multi-line symbol. Drains (D) use a drop or 'D' notation.

questions.stem: A pressure vessel drawing specifies a nozzle location as 'NPS 4, Sch 80, elevation 1500 mm from bottom TL, 90° from N azimuth'. What does 'TL' mean?

choices.C: Tangent line — the point where the head-to-shell junction begins

questions.explanation: TL = Tangent Line. On a pressure vessel, this is the reference line where a curved head (elliptical, hemispherical, torispherical) meets the cylindrical shell. All vertical dimensions on the vessel are typically referenced to bottom TL. ASME Section VIII uses this convention throughout.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of a jig or fixture in weld fabrication?

choices.A: To speed up welding by eliminating quality checks
choices.C: To hold parts in the correct position and alignment, and often to restrain distortion, during welding

questions.explanation: Jigs and fixtures hold parts in correct alignment and often provide the mass/restraint needed to control distortion. They improve consistency, reduce measurement time on repeat parts, and can incorporate quick-clamps for productivity. They do not replace inspection (A), the welder (B), or measurement of the finished part (D).

questions.stem: When fitting two plates for a butt joint, which measurement is checked with a taper gauge or wedge?

choices.A: Root opening (gap between the two plates)

questions.explanation: A taper gauge or step wedge is designed to measure the root opening — the gap between prepared edges at the root. Thickness (B) uses a micrometer or caliper. Flatness (C) uses a straightedge and feeler gauge. Bevel angle (D) uses a bevel protractor or template.

questions.stem: Two 12 mm plates are being fit up for a single-V groove weld with 3 mm root opening. The gap is measured as 5 mm along one edge. What is the correct action?

choices.A: Accept the gap — it will fill in during welding
choices.C: Correct the fit-up (adjust clamping, add backing, or trim) to bring root opening within the WPS tolerance before welding

questions.explanation: Root opening is an essential variable on most WPSs. A gap outside tolerance can cause burn-through, weld-metal cracking, and incomplete penetration. The correct step is always to fix fit-up before welding. Filling gaps with weld metal is called 'buttering' and is only allowed by specific WPS provisions; even then it must be documented. Grinding after (D) can't fix an out-of-tolerance root.

questions.stem: Which distortion-control technique involves welding a joint in short segments that skip ahead, then returning to fill the gaps?

choices.C: Skip welding (also called wandering or intermittent sequence)

questions.explanation: Skip (wandering) welding deposits short segments spaced along the joint, then returns to fill between them. This spreads heat input over time and reduces continuous longitudinal contraction. Back-step (A) welds short lengths against the direction of travel. Cascade (B) is a multi-pass sequencing technique. Vertical-up (D) is a position, not a distortion technique.

questions.stem: What is 'back-step welding'?

choices.B: Removing weld metal in preparation for the next pass
choices.D: Depositing short weld lengths whose direction of travel is opposite to the overall welding progression

questions.explanation: Back-step welding: the welder makes a short bead ending at the start point of the previous bead, then jumps ahead and welds another short bead back to the previous start. The overall direction of progression is opposite to the direction of each short bead. This is a distortion-control technique that spreads and cancels contraction forces.

questions.stem: A fabricated I-beam shows angular distortion — the flanges have rotated inward after the fillet welds attaching them to the web cooled. Which of these is the best mitigation for the next assembly?

choices.A: Weld both fillets simultaneously with two welders
choices.B: Weld only one side and leave the other unwelded
choices.C: Pre-set the flanges rotated outward by an estimated amount so they return to square after welding, and/or weld with balanced passes on alternating sides

questions.explanation: The two standard responses to predictable angular distortion are (1) pre-set — cambering or angling the assembly opposite the expected distortion so it returns to true after welding — and (2) balanced welding — alternating passes on opposite sides of the neutral axis so contraction forces cancel. Simultaneous welding with two operators (A) can help but is often impractical; single-side welding (B) doesn't complete the joint; larger fillets (D) worsen distortion.

sources.ref: Distortion control — pre-setting and balanced welding

questions.stem: In fit-up terminology, what is a 'backing bar' (or 'backing strip')?

choices.A: A strip of material placed at the root of a groove weld to support molten weld metal during the root pass
choices.B: A stiffener welded across the back of a distorted assembly
choices.C: A tool used to grind out defects

questions.explanation: A backing bar is a strip (often mild steel matching base metal, or ceramic, or copper) placed at the root to support molten metal on the first pass and allow full penetration without burn-through. Steel backing may be left in place (as part of the joint per WPS) or removed after welding. Ceramic backing is removed. Copper is used when heat must be sunk away — never fused.

questions.stem: For a fillet weld, what is the 'throat' dimension?

choices.B: The shortest distance from the joint root to the weld face (theoretical throat = leg × 0.707 for equal-leg 90° fillet)

questions.explanation: Fillet weld strength is calculated on the throat, not the leg. For an equal-leg 90° fillet, theoretical throat = leg × sin(45°) = leg × 0.707. Actual throat (measured) may differ due to convexity/concavity of the face. CSA W59 and AWS D1.1 use throat area × filler metal shear strength for capacity calculations.

questions.stem: A 10 mm equal-leg fillet weld is specified. What is the theoretical throat and approximate deposited weld-metal cross-section per unit length?

choices.D: Throat 7.07 mm, area ≈ 50 mm² (per mm of length)

questions.explanation: Throat = 10 × 0.707 = 7.07 mm. Cross-section of the triangle = ½ × leg × leg = ½ × 10 × 10 = 50 mm² per mm of length. This value is used for deposit rate and consumable estimating. Options A and B express the same numbers; B is the properly-stated per-mm length form.

questions.stem: A structural connection requires an 8 mm fillet weld continuous around a 100 × 200 mm rectangular hollow section, both sides of a base plate. What is the total length of weld?
questions.explanation: Perimeter of 100 × 200 = 2(100+200) = 600 mm per side. 'Both sides of a base plate' typically means the HSS is only welded on the outside of the connection (from one accessible side); 'both sides of the base plate' as written would double it to 1200. In common practice, an HSS to base-plate connection welds only the exposed perimeter = 600 mm. Answer D accepts the standard reading; D reflects the doubled reading if truly two-sided. When ambiguous, always confirm with the drawing.

questions.stem: In estimating consumable use, deposition efficiency (DE) accounts for what?

choices.A: The number of welds per hour
choices.B: The percentage of purchased filler metal that ends up as sound weld metal in the joint, after losses to spatter, slag, stubs, and burn-off
choices.C: The percentage of joints that pass inspection
choices.D: The efficiency of the power source

questions.explanation: Deposition efficiency = mass of weld metal deposited / mass of consumable purchased. Typical values: SMAW ≈ 55–65% (stubs, slag, spatter), FCAW ≈ 75–85%, GMAW ≈ 85–95%, SAW ≈ 95%+. Multiply required deposit weight by 1/DE to estimate purchase quantity. This is separate from joint pass rate (C) and power efficiency (D).

questions.stem: A job requires 25 kg of deposited weld metal using SMAW E7018 with an assumed deposition efficiency of 60%. How much filler metal must be purchased?
questions.explanation: Purchase quantity = deposit ÷ DE = 25 ÷ 0.60 ≈ 41.7 kg. Round up to 42 kg (or a full carton). Answer A applies DE the wrong direction; B ignores losses; D confuses percentage.

questions.stem: The same job in the previous question is quoted for labour at 3 kg/hour deposition rate. What is the estimated arc-on time?
questions.explanation: Arc-on time = deposit weight ÷ deposition rate = 25 ÷ 3 ≈ 8.3 hours. This is arc-on only — actual labour hours are higher due to operator factor (arc-on time as % of shift, typically 20–40% for SMAW). Answer C reflects labour hours assuming a low operator factor.

questions.stem: What is 'operator factor' or 'arc time factor'?

choices.B: The percentage of total shift time during which the arc is actually burning (typical 20–40% for manual processes, higher for semi-automatic and mechanized)
choices.C: The number of welders on a crew

questions.explanation: Operator factor accounts for setup, movement, electrode changes, chipping/cleaning between passes, and non-weld activities. SMAW is typically 20–30%; FCAW/GMAW 30–40%; mechanized 60%+. Understanding operator factor is critical for accurate labour estimation and shop planning.

questions.stem: What is 'peening' in a welding context?

choices.D: Mechanical working of the weld surface with a hammer, needle scaler, or shot to induce compressive stress

questions.explanation: Peening plastically deforms the weld surface, inducing compressive residual stress that offsets the tensile residual stress from cooling. Used judiciously (typically intermediate passes on thick sections, not root or cap), it can reduce distortion and improve fatigue life. Overuse causes work hardening. CSA W59 and AWS D1.1 restrict peening on root and final passes.

questions.stem: A fabricator needs to straighten a distorted structural angle after welding. Which method uses controlled localized heating to create shrinkage that reverses the distortion?

choices.B: Flame straightening (heat-shrinking) using localized torch heating

questions.explanation: Flame (heat) straightening uses localized heating in patterns (spot, line, or wedge) to create controlled shrinkage as the heated area cools while restrained. The heated area yields in compression when hot, then contracts on cooling to pull the piece straight. Temperatures are kept below the metal's lower critical (typically 550–650°C for structural steel) to avoid metallurgical changes. Cold press (A) is possible but often not feasible on complex shapes; cryogenic (C) is not standard; hammering (D) is uncontrolled.

sources.ref: Heat straightening of welded structural steel

questions.stem: A welder is instructed to heat-straighten a distorted A514 (quenched and tempered) beam member. What is the primary concern that makes this different from heat-straightening a plain A36 member?

choices.B: A514's mechanical properties depend on its heat treatment; exceeding approximately 590°C can temper it further and reduce yield/tensile strength permanently. Maximum straightening temperature is strictly controlled (typically ~590°C max) and closely monitored
choices.C: A514 cannot be heat-straightened at all
choices.D: A514 requires higher temperatures than A36

questions.explanation: Q&T steels like A514, A517, and HSLA plates lose strength if reheated above their tempering temperature. AWS D1.1 and manufacturer guidance limit maximum heat-straightening temperature on Q&T steels to about 590°C, with temperature-indicating crayons/pyrometers used to confirm. Exceeding this permanently reduces yield strength, which for A514's ~690 MPa yield can drop it toward A36 levels — potentially unsafe in service.

questions.stem: What is 'arc gouging' typically used for in fabrication?

choices.A: Removing defective weld metal, back-gouging root passes prior to welding the second side, and preparing joints

questions.explanation: Arc gouging (typically CAC-A — carbon arc with compressed air) removes metal by melting and blowing away with air. Common uses: back-gouging groove-weld roots before welding the second side to ensure full penetration, removing defective weld sections identified by NDE, and preparing joints where mechanical cutting is impractical. It is not for finish cutting (C, use OFC/PAC) or scrap melting (D).

sources.ref: Air carbon arc gouging and cutting

questions.stem: After back-gouging a groove weld root using CAC-A, what surface preparation is required before welding the back side?

choices.A: Grind the gouged surface to remove carbon deposits and any heat-affected/carburized layer, back to clean metal, before welding

questions.explanation: CAC-A can leave carbon deposits from the electrode and a thin carburized surface layer on the gouged metal. If not removed, this can cause weld defects — porosity, cracking (from higher-carbon HAZ), and inclusions. AWS D1.1 and CSA W59 require grinding the gouged surface back to bright clean metal before welding.

questions.stem: In an AWS A2.4 symbol, what does a small flag at the elbow of the reference line indicate?

choices.D: Field weld (to be made on site, not in the shop)

questions.explanation: A flag at the elbow (junction of arrow and reference line) means field weld. A circle at the elbow means weld all around. Full penetration is shown by 'CJP' notation or specific groove symbol conventions. Machine finish uses the finish symbol on the weld itself.

questions.stem: For fitting a nozzle to a pressure vessel shell, what fit-up check confirms the nozzle is perpendicular to the vessel surface?

choices.C: Weight the nozzle so it settles by gravity
choices.D: Use a level, square, or contour-following template to measure squareness in two planes, and check clearance around the entire nozzle-to-shell fit

questions.explanation: Nozzle squareness on a curved shell must be verified in two orthogonal planes (longitudinal and circumferential axes of the vessel) using appropriate tools. Contour templates that match the shell's curvature help confirm even fit-up all around. Visual (A) is insufficient for pressure work. Gravity (C) doesn't guarantee square on a curved surface. Trusting drawings (B) skips required inspection.
